timeline.title: Physiographic Evolution Milestones
timeline.description: The sequential geological phases that sculpted India's modern physiographic landscape.

cards.details: Consolidation of the ancient Aravalli, Singhbhum, and Dharwar cratons, forming the bedrock shield of the Peninsular Plateau.
Tectonic downfaulting in the Peninsula created grabens (Damodar, Mahanadi, Godavari) accumulating rich plant matter which formed Gondwana coal.
Massive flood basalt eruptions covered the north-western Peninsula, creating the flat-topped stepped Deccan Trap landscape.
Three distinct folding phases uplifted the Trans-Himalayas, Greater Himalayas, Lesser Himalayas, and finally the Shiwaliks.
Accumulation of massive sediment volumes in the foredeep basin between the rising Himalayas and the stable shield, forming the fertile Northern Plains.

traps.title: UPSC Common Exam Traps
items: Trap 1: Meghalaya Plateau Connection: The Meghalaya (Shillong) Plateau and Karbi Anglong are NOT part of the Himalayas. They are geologically extensions of the **Peninsular Plateau**, separated from it by the Malda Fault (Garo-Rajmahal Gap).

Trap 2: Western vs Eastern Ghats Continuity: A common trap is assuming both Ghats are continuous. The **Western Ghats are continuous** and can be crossed only through passes, while the **Eastern Ghats are highly dissected, discontinuous**, and broken by major east-flowing rivers (Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri).

Trap 3: Bhabar vs Terai Characteristics: Bhabar is a dry, porous belt of gravels where streams disappear. Terai is a wet, swampy, marshy forest belt just south of Bhabar where streams re-emerge. Confusing these two is a classic UPSC trap.

Trap 4: Island Origins: Lakshadweep islands are of **coral origin** (built up by polyps), whereas the Andaman and Nicobar islands are of **tectonic/volcanic origin** (submarine tertiary mountain ranges rising from the ocean floor).

deepDive.title: Syllabus Core Study Notes (Deep-Dive)
deepDive.description: Geographical classifications, mountain structures, plateau systems, and coastal divisions.

sections.title: 1. The Northern Mountains (Himalayas & Purvanchal)
sections.content:
The Northern Mountains are divided into the Trans-Himalayas, the Himalayan mountain range, and the Purvanchal (Eastern Hills).

Structural Ranges (N to S)
  • Trans-Himalayas: Karakoram, Ladakh, and Zaskar ranges. Mostly dry, cold desert conditions.
  • Greater Himalayas (Himadri): Highest peaks (Everest, Kanchenjunga). Continuous, composed of granite core.
  • Lesser Himalayas (Himachal): Pir Panjal, Dhauladhar, Mahabharat ranges. Highly rugged, famous hill stations.
  • Outer Himalayas (Shiwaliks): Youngest range, made of consolidated sediments, characterized by flat valleys called **Duns** (e.g., Dehradun).
Regional Divisions (W to E)
  • Kashmir/Western Himalayas: Famous for Karewa formations (saffron), cold deserts.
  • Kumaon Himalayas: Between Satluj and Kali rivers; contains peaks like Nanda Devi.
  • Sikkim-Darjeeling Himalayas: Fast-flowing rivers, orchid flora, tea plantations.
  • Arunachal/Eastern Himalayas: High rainfall, deep gorges, home to tribes.
  • Purvanchal: Patkai Bum, Naga Hills, Manipur Hills, and Mizo Hills.

sections.title: 2. The Northern Plains & The Peninsular Plateau
sections.content:
The Plains and the Plateau form the agricultural and mineral backbone of India, respectively.

The Northern Plains (Sub-regions)
  • Bhabar: Porous gravel zone at foothills. Rivers run underground.
  • Terai: Swampy zone where rivers re-emerge; rich in biodiversity.
  • Bhangar: Older clayey alluvium forming upland terraces. Contains calcium nodules called **kankar**.
  • Khadar: Young, fertile alluvial silt renewed annually by floods.
The Peninsular Plateau (Sub-units)
  • Central Highlands: Malwa Plateau, Bundelkhand, Baghelkhand. Bordered by Aravalli and Vindhyan ranges.
  • Deccan Plateau: Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Telangana plateaus. Stepped basalt topography.
  • Northeastern Extension: Meghalaya (Garo, Khasi, Jaintia hills) and Mikir hills. Structurally part of Peninsular block.
  • Chotanagpur Plateau: Rich in minerals (coal, iron). Damodar valley coal graben.

sections.title: 3. Coastal Plains, Western & Eastern Ghats, and Islands
sections.content:
The coastal tracts, mountain borders, and oceanic islands form distinct ecological and structural zones.

Western vs Eastern Ghats
  • Western Ghats (Sahyadris): High, continuous, steep western slope. Thal Ghat, Bhor Ghat, and Pal Ghat are key passes. Highest peak: **Anamudi**.
  • Eastern Ghats: Discontinuous, highly dissected by east-flowing rivers. Average elevation is lower. Highest peak: **Jindhagada / Mahendragiri**.
Coasts and Islands
  • Western Coastal Plains: Narrow, submergent coast. Divided into Konkan, Kannad, and Malabar coasts. Features lagoons (Kayals).
  • Eastern Coastal Plains: Broad, emergent coast. Divided into Northern Circars and Coromandel coast. Famous for large river deltas.
  • Islands: Andaman & Nicobar (tectonic upliftment, volcanic activity like Barren Island) and Lakshadweep (atoll coral islands in the Arabian Sea).

mockTestQuestions.q: Which of the following mountain ranges is NOT a part of the Trans-Himalayan zone?
mockTestQuestions.sol: The Pir Panjal Range is the longest and most important range of the Lesser Himalayas (Himachal), not the Trans-Himalayan zone.

mockTestQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the Meghalaya Plateau:
1. It is a geological extension of the Peninsular Plateau of India.
2. It is separated from the main Peninsular block by the Malda Fault.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
mockTestQuestions.sol: Both statements are correct. The Shillong/Meghalaya Plateau is an outlier of the Peninsular shield, separated from the Rajmahal hills by the tectonic Malda fault gap (Garo-Rajmahal Gap).

mockTestQuestions.q: The Bhabar belt along the foothills of the Shiwalik range is characterized by:
opts: Highly clayey, marshy, and waterlogged soil
Coarse gravel and boulder deposits where small streams disappear
Older alluvial terraces containing calcareous kankar
Vast tracts of sand dunes subject to wind erosion
mockTestQuestions.sol: Bhabar is a narrow porous belt of gravels and boulders at the Shiwalik foothills. Due to high permeability, streams sink and flow underground.

mockTestQuestions.q: Which of the following passes connects Mumbai with Pune through the Western Ghats?
mockTestQuestions.sol: Bhor Ghat connects Mumbai with Pune, while Thal Ghat connects Mumbai with Nashik.

mockTestQuestions.q: Why are the Western Coastal Plains narrow and characterized by estuaries, while the Eastern Coastal Plains are broad with large deltas?
opts: The Western coast is an emergent coast with high wave energy.
The Western coast is a submergent coast, and Western Ghats rivers have short, steep courses, carrying less silt.
The Eastern coast has no major rivers flowing into the sea.
The Earth's rotation tilts all silt deposits toward the East.
mockTestQuestions.sol: The western coast is submergent, and the steep slope of the Western Ghats means rivers flow fast, have short courses, and carry little sediment, forming estuaries instead of deltas. The eastern coast is emergent with broad deltas from massive silt-carrying rivers.

mockTestQuestions.q: Which channel separates the Andaman Islands from the Nicobar Islands?
mockTestQuestions.sol: The Ten Degree Channel separates the Andaman group of islands from the Nicobar group in the Bay of Bengal.

mockTestQuestions.q: The highest peak of the Peninsular Plateau of India is:
mockTestQuestions.sol: Anamudi (2,695m) in the Anaimalai Hills of Kerala is the highest peak of the Peninsular Plateau and South India.

mockTestQuestions.q: Which physiographic sub-unit is also known as the 'Ruhr of India' due to its vast mineral wealth?
mockTestQuestions.sol: The Chotanagpur Plateau is rich in metallics, non-metallics, and coal, making it the mineral heart or 'Ruhr of India'.

mockTestQuestions.q: The flat valleys lying between the Lesser Himalayas and the Shiwalik range are geologically known as:
mockTestQuestions.sol: Duns are longitudinal structural valleys formed between the Lesser Himalayas and Shiwaliks (e.g., Dehra Dun, Patli Dun).

mockTestQuestions.q: The Lakshadweep Islands in the Arabian Sea are geologically categorized as:
opts: Volcanic islands formed by a hotspot plume
Atoll coral islands built on a submerged ridge
Submerged extensions of the Western Ghats
mockTestQuestions.sol: Lakshadweep consists of coral islands, mostly atolls, built on the Laccadive-Chagos submarine ridge.
